title: Being and Becoming in Modern Physics

summaries.example: Imagine a school hallway with rooms in a row. In one view, only the room you are in exists right now. In another, the rooms you have passed still exist, while rooms ahead are only possibilities. In a third, every room exists, and “the room you are in” depends on where you are. Philosophers use similar pictures to think about the past, present, and future.
summaries.summary: This entry explores an old question: what are the past, present, and future like? One view says only the present exists. Another says the past and present are real, while the future is still open. A third says all times are real, like different places on a map. Newtonian physics gives everyone the same broad present. Special relativity makes the issue harder because people moving differently can disagree about which distant events are happening at the same time. The entry also examines arguments that time cannot really pass and explains why physics may describe events without capturing everything people mean by the feeling of “now.” It does not settle the disagreement, but it shows how modern physics makes the questions sharper.
key_ideas: People have long disagreed about whether time truly flows and whether the future is already real.
Presentism, possibilism, and eternalism give different answers about what exists.
Newtonian physics allows one shared present, but special relativity says that simultaneity can depend on motion.
Some philosophers argue that the feeling of a moving present may be about our viewpoint rather than a feature physics must describe.
Explaining passage as time moving like an object creates difficult questions, such as what time would move with respect to.
summaries.why_it_matters: Our ideas about time affect how we think about change, choice, the future, and what it means for something to exist. Physics gives important information about clocks, events, motion, and signals, but philosophers still ask how that information connects with everyday experience. Learning the different views helps us separate what a theory measures from what people mean when they say that time is passing.

important_terms.definition: The idea that only what is happening right now exists. The past no longer exists, and the future does not exist yet.
The idea that the past and present exist, while the future is made of possibilities that may become real.
The idea that past, present, and future events are all equally real. The present is not more real than the past or future.
The idea that time changes or “moves,” so events become present and then become past.
A way of showing the history of an object or person through spacetime.
The idea that two events happen at the same time. In Newtonian physics, this can be the same for everyone.

questions_to_think_about: If only the present exists, what happens to yesterday when it is no longer happening?
Would two people moving differently always agree about what is happening right now?
Can a map of all events show change without the map itself moving?
Is your experience of “now” the same thing as a scientific fact about the universe?

summaries.example: Suppose Alice and Bob pass one another on Earth while walking in opposite directions toward and away from a distant galaxy. Special relativity assigns them different planes of simultaneity. A launch in that galaxy could fall in Alice’s past but in Bob’s future, even though the launch cannot causally affect their meeting. This example challenges the idea that one distant, universal present determines which events already exist.
summaries.summary: The entry examines the metaphysics of time through classical and relativistic spacetime. In Newtonian spacetime, temporal intervals and simultaneity are absolute, allowing three familiar positions: presentism, possibilism, and eternalism. Presentism identifies reality with the present; possibilism treats the past as actual and the future as open; eternalism treats all times as equally real. McTaggart’s A-series/B-series distinction frames a major argument that passage is contradictory, although later discussion questions whether the contradiction results from ambiguity in tense and existence. Special relativity changes the setting. Because simultaneity is frame-relative, no inertial frame is physically singled out as containing the universal present. This motivates arguments for a block universe, but the source stresses that coordinate assignments to spacelike-separated events do not by themselves establish metaphysical fixity or causal determination. Alternative accounts seek local becoming through light cones, proper time, world lines, or finite “present” regions. The entry presents these options without claiming that one final solution has been established.
key_ideas: The central dispute concerns whether temporal passage is an objective feature of reality, a feature of perspective, or an incoherent idea.
McTaggart distinguished a changing A-series from the fixed B-series and argued that the A-series involves a contradiction; later philosophers dispute both his assumptions and his reasoning.
In Newtonian spacetime, simultaneity is absolute, so presentism and possibilism have a natural global slice on which to build.
Special relativity provides no frame-independent global present: inertial frames disagree about simultaneity for spacelike-separated events.
The Andromeda-style argument suggests a troubling form of chronogeometrical fatalism, but the source argues that spacelike-separated events cannot causally determine one another.
Proposals influenced by Stein and others understand becoming locally, using light-cone relations, proper time, world lines, or finite local regions rather than a universal present.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue connects metaphysics with the structure of physical theories. It asks whether scientific descriptions of spacetime settle questions about existence, openness of the future, and passage, or whether those questions require additional philosophical interpretation. It also illustrates a broader lesson: concepts that seem united in ordinary life—presentness, simultaneity, existence, and becoming—can separate when examined in a precise physical framework.

important_terms.definition: The metaphysical thesis that only present events exist; past events no longer exist and future events do not yet exist.
The view that the past and present are actual, while the future consists of possibilities that have not yet become actual; it is also called the growing-block view.
The view that past, present, and future events are all equally part of reality, with no universal ontological privilege for the present.
McTaggart’s name for the ordering of events as future, present, and past, whose properties appear to change.
McTaggart’s name for the fixed ordering in which one event is earlier or later than another.
The claim in special relativity that distant simultaneity depends on the inertial frame used to describe events.
A spacetime structure determined by the invariant speed of light, separating events into timelike, lightlike, and spacelike relations.
Time measured along a particular timelike world line, such as the path of an ideal clock; unlike coordinate time, it is not frame-dependent.

questions_to_think_about: Does the relativity of simultaneity refute presentism, or does it show only that presentism needs a different formulation?
Is McTaggart’s contradiction genuine, or does it depend on shifting meanings of words such as “is” or “exists”?
Why does spacelike separation weaken the inference from one observer’s past to another observer’s fixed future?
Can a local present count as genuine temporal passage if it contains only one event or a small region?
What, if anything, would physics need to add in order to distinguish a real passage of time from a static spacetime description?

summaries.example: Picture two students, Maya and Leo, passing each other while looking toward a faraway planet. Because they are moving in opposite directions, relativity allows them to disagree about which distant event is happening at the same time as their meeting. A decision on the planet might be in Maya’s past but Leo’s future. This does not mean either student caused the decision; the distant event is too far away for a signal to connect it to their meeting.
summaries.summary: This entry asks how modern physics can help us think about time, change, and existence. It compares three views. Presentism says only the present exists. Possibilism says the past and present exist, while the future remains open. Eternalism says every time is real, making the present no more special than a distant place. In Newtonian physics, everyone can share one system of simultaneous events. McTaggart’s famous argument claims that the changing past-present-future pattern is inconsistent, although the entry discusses possible replies involving the meanings of tense and existence. Special relativity introduces a major complication: observers moving differently can disagree about distant simultaneity. This supports some arguments for a block universe, but it does not automatically prove that every event is causally fixed. Since events outside one another’s light cones cannot influence each other in the ordinary relativistic picture, some philosophers develop local accounts of becoming using light-cone relations, world lines, and proper time.
key_ideas: The question “Does time pass?” has both a scientific side and a philosophical side.
Newtonian spacetime supports a single shared ordering of simultaneous events.
The three main metaphysical views disagree about whether the future exists and whether the present is special.
McTaggart argued that describing events as future, present, and past leads to trouble, but philosophers disagree about whether his argument succeeds.
Special relativity makes a universal present difficult because simultaneity is not the same for every inertial observer.
Some proposals replace a global present with local relations involving light cones or the time measured along an object’s path.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate shows why everyday words can become difficult in science and philosophy. “Now,” “real,” and “before” seem simple, but their meanings can change depending on whether we are discussing experience, language, Newtonian physics, or relativity. Studying these views helps us understand both the power and the limits of scientific models, while showing why disagreements can remain reasonable even when everyone accepts the same physical theory.

important_terms.definition: The view that only the present is real. The past has stopped existing, and the future has not begun to exist.
The view that the past and present are real, while the future is not yet actual. It is often pictured as a block that grows.
The view that all times are real, so past and future events are not less real simply because they are not present.
A pattern of events described as future, present, and past. It is meant to represent time’s changing aspect.
A permanent ordering of events by earlier-than and later-than relations.
The fact that observers in different states of motion may disagree about which distant events are simultaneous.
The path of an object or person through spacetime, showing its changing locations and times.
The region around an event that can be reached by, or can send, light or slower-moving matter. It helps identify possible causal connections.

questions_to_think_about: Which view best matches the difference between remembering the past and predicting the future?
Does disagreement about distant simultaneity show that there is no real present, or only that “present” must be used locally?
Why might a fixed ordering of events fail to capture the feeling that things are changing?
What is gained and lost by describing becoming with light cones instead of a universal time slice?
